chapters.title: Unit 1: Introduction to AI
chapters.content:
Unit 1: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

12 Marks — Master every concept here for guaranteed marks.

What is Intelligence?

Intelligence is the ability to learn, reason, solve problems, perceive the environment, and use language effectively.

Think of it like this: A calculator can add numbers, but it cannot decide which numbers to add. Intelligence is what fills that gap — the ability to make decisions, adapt, and learn from experience.

Components of Intelligence

  • Learning — Acquiring new knowledge from experience (e.g., a child learns that fire is hot by touching it once)
  • Reasoning — Drawing conclusions from known facts (e.g., "All humans die. Socrates is human. Therefore Socrates will die.")
  • Problem Solving — Finding solutions to complex situations (e.g., finding the shortest route on a map)
  • Perception — Understanding the environment through senses (e.g., recognizing a face, hearing music)
  • Using Language — Communicating meaningfully (e.g., understanding the difference between "I saw the man with binoculars" — who has the binoculars?)

What is Artificial Intelligence?

AI Definition: Artificial Intelligence is the simulation of human intelligence in machines that are programmed to think, learn, and solve problems like humans.

"AI is the science and engineering of making intelligent machines." — John McCarthy (Father of AI, coined the term in 1956)

Simple Analogy

Think of AI like teaching a dog tricks. The dog (machine) learns through training (data) to respond correctly to commands (inputs). The smarter and more varied the training, the better the dog performs — even in new situations.

Human Intelligence vs Artificial Intelligence

AspectHuman IntelligenceArtificial Intelligence
LearningLearns from experience naturallyLearns from data and training
SpeedRelatively slowExtremely fast processing
AccuracyMakes emotional/cognitive errorsHighly accurate if trained well
CreativityCan be truly creativeLimited/simulated creativity
EmotionHas emotionsNo real emotions (simulated)
AdaptabilityAdapts to completely new situationsStruggles with truly novel situations
CostOngoing (salary, food, rest)One-time hardware/software cost
MultitaskingLimitedCan run thousands of tasks simultaneously

Goals of AI

  • Replicate human intelligence — Make machines that think and act as humans do
  • Solve complex problems — Problems too large or fast for humans (e.g., weather prediction, drug discovery)
  • Expert performance — Perform tasks at or beyond expert human level (chess, medical diagnosis)
  • Reduce human effort — Automate repetitive dangerous or boring tasks
  • Improve decision making — Provide data-driven decisions in business, healthcare, governance

Foundational Disciplines of AI

AI is interdisciplinary — it draws from many fields:

DisciplineContribution to AI
PhilosophyConcepts of mind, knowledge, reasoning, ethics
MathematicsLogic, probability, statistics, optimization
PsychologyHow humans think, learn, and behave
Computer EngineeringHardware to run AI systems
LinguisticsNatural language understanding and generation
Biological ScienceNeural networks inspired by brain biology

Evolution of AI — Timeline

  • 1943 — McCulloch & Pitts propose the first mathematical model of a neuron
  • 1950 — Alan Turing proposes the Turing Test in his paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence"
  • 1956 — John McCarthy coins the term "Artificial Intelligence" at the Dartmouth Conference
  • 1957 — Frank Rosenblatt invents the Perceptron (first neural network)
  • 1960s–70s — Early AI programs: ELIZA (chatbot), DENDRAL (chemistry expert system)
  • 1970s–80s — AI Winter #1: funding cuts due to unmet expectations
  • 1980s — Expert Systems boom — rule-based systems for specific domains
  • 1987–93 — AI Winter #2: expert systems too costly to maintain
  • 1997 — IBM's Deep Blue defeats chess world champion Garry Kasparov
  • 2011 — IBM's Watson wins Jeopardy! quiz show
  • 2012 — Deep Learning revolution begins (AlexNet wins ImageNet)
  • 2016 — Google's AlphaGo defeats world Go champion
  • 2022 — ChatGPT launches, making AI accessible to everyone

Symbolic AI

Symbolic AI (also called Good Old-Fashioned AI / GOFAI) is the approach where intelligence is represented through symbols and rules, like human language and logic.

Example: An expert system for medical diagnosis has rules like:
IF temperature > 38.5 AND cough = true THEN possible_diagnosis = flu

Advantages: Explainable, works well for well-defined domains
Disadvantages: Cannot handle uncertainty, requires manual rule creation, doesn't scale

AI Winters — Why Did Progress Stop?

An AI Winter is a period when AI research slows drastically due to loss of funding and interest, usually because promises exceeded actual capabilities.

  • 1st Winter (1974–80): Computers were too slow, couldn't store enough data, and early programs failed on real-world complexity
  • 2nd Winter (1987–93): Expert systems were too expensive to maintain and couldn't generalize
AI Winters are important to understand because they show that overpromising AI capabilities leads to loss of trust. The key lesson: AI progress is incremental, not a sudden explosion.

Risks and Benefits of AI

Benefits

  • Healthcare: Earlier and more accurate diagnosis (cancer detection)
  • Automation of dangerous jobs (bomb disposal robots)
  • 24/7 availability (customer service chatbots)
  • Scientific discovery acceleration (AlphaFold solved protein folding)
  • Personalization (Netflix recommendations, Spotify playlists)

Risks

  • Job displacement: Many routine jobs may be automated
  • Bias: AI trained on biased data perpetuates discrimination
  • Privacy: Mass surveillance using facial recognition
  • Autonomous weapons: Lethal decisions without human oversight
  • Dependency: Over-reliance reducing human skill
  • Existential risk: Super-intelligent AI acting against human values (theoretical)

Major Subfields of AI

SubfieldWhat it DoesExample
Machine LearningSystems that learn from data without explicit programmingEmail spam filter
Neural NetworksLayers of artificial neurons inspired by the brainImage recognition
Machine VisionInterpreting and understanding visual informationSelf-driving cars
RoboticsAI applied to physical machines that interact with the worldSurgical robots
Expert SystemsAI that simulates decision-making of a human expertMedical diagnosis system
Natural Language ProcessingUnderstanding and generating human languageGoogle Translate, ChatGPT

Exam Questions & Answers — Unit 1

Q1: Define Artificial Intelligence. What are its goals?

Answer: AI is the branch of computer science that deals with creating machines capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence. Goals include: automating tasks, solving complex problems, improving decision-making, and replicating human cognitive abilities.

Q2: Differentiate between Human Intelligence and Artificial Intelligence. (6 marks)

Answer: Use the table above. Key differences: AI is faster but lacks creativity/emotion; HI is adaptive but slower and error-prone.

Q3: What are AI Winters? Why did they occur?

Answer: AI Winters are periods of reduced funding and interest in AI research. They occurred because early AI systems failed to meet the overhyped expectations. The gap between theoretical promise and practical capability led governments and corporations to withdraw funding.

Q4: Name and briefly explain the foundational disciplines of AI.

Answer: Philosophy (reasoning), Mathematics (logic, probability), Psychology (cognition), Computer Engineering (hardware), Linguistics (language understanding), Biological Science (neural inspiration). Each discipline provides tools and concepts that AI borrows and integrates.

Q5: What is Symbolic AI? What are its limitations?

Answer: Symbolic AI uses symbols and rules to represent knowledge. Limitation: cannot handle uncertainty, requires manual rule creation, doesn't learn from data, fails in complex real-world scenarios.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Intelligent Agents
chapters.content:
Unit 2: Intelligent Agents and Environments

12 Marks

The Four Views of AI

AI systems can be classified by what they try to achieve and how they do it:

ViewGoalMeasureExample
Acting HumanlyBehave like a humanTuring TestChatbots, voice assistants
Thinking HumanlyThink like a human (cognitive modeling)Cognitive science experimentsACT-R cognitive architecture
Acting RationallyDo the right thing to achieve goalsRationality (best expected outcome)Chess engines, pathfinding
Thinking RationallyUse correct logic and reasoningLaws of thoughtTheorem provers, Prolog

The Turing Test — Explained Simply

Alan Turing proposed: If a machine can have a conversation with a human and the human cannot tell it is a machine, the machine is intelligent.

Setup: A human interrogator types questions. Responses come from either a human or a machine. If the interrogator cannot reliably identify which is which after 5 minutes, the machine passes.

Criticism: Passing the Turing Test does not necessarily mean the machine truly understands — it might just be very good at mimicking. (Chinese Room Argument by John Searle)

What is an Agent?

An agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators.

Environment → [Sensors] → Agent (Perceive → Think → Decide) → [Actuators] → Environment

Examples of Agents

Agent TypeSensorsActuators
HumanEyes, ears, nose, skinHands, legs, mouth
RobotCameras, microphones, sonarMotors, wheels, grippers
Software agentKeyboard input, files, networkScreen output, files, network
Self-driving carCameras, LIDAR, GPSSteering, brakes, accelerator

Types of AI Agents

1. Simple Reflex Agent

How it works: Acts based ONLY on the current percept. Has a set of condition-action rules (IF-THEN).

IF dirt is perceived THEN suck
IF no dirt THEN move forward

Pros: Simple, fast
Cons: Cannot handle situations not covered by rules. Has no memory — no idea what happened before.

Real Example: A thermostat — IF temperature < 20°C THEN turn on heater.

2. Model-Based Reflex Agent

How it works: Maintains an internal model (memory) of the world. Uses current percept + memory to decide action.

State = update_state(state, action, percept, model)
Action = rule_match(state, rules)

Pros: Can handle partially observable environments
Cons: Internal model may become inaccurate over time

Real Example: A robot vacuum that remembers which rooms it has cleaned.

3. Goal-Based Agent

How it works: Has a goal and evaluates actions based on whether they help achieve that goal. Uses search and planning.

Pros: Flexible — can adapt to different goals
Cons: More complex, slower decision-making

Real Example: A GPS navigation system — it has the goal "reach destination" and plans the route accordingly.

4. Utility-Based Agent

How it works: Uses a utility function to measure how desirable each state is. Chooses actions that maximize expected utility.

Why needed? Sometimes multiple actions can achieve the goal — utility helps choose the BEST one.

Real Example: A self-driving car that must choose between routes — it uses utility to balance speed, safety, fuel, and comfort.

5. Learning Agent

How it works: Learns from experience to improve performance over time. Has 4 components:

  • Learning element — Makes improvements by learning from feedback
  • Performance element — Selects actions (the "brain")
  • Critic — Evaluates performance against a performance standard
  • Problem generator — Suggests new experiences to explore

Real Example: AlphaGo — it started knowing only the rules of Go and learned by playing millions of games against itself.

Agent Environments

The environment is everything outside the agent that it perceives and acts upon. Environments are categorized by several properties:

Task Environment = PEAS

Every AI problem can be described using PEAS:

  • Performance measure — How do we judge success?
  • Environment — What does the agent operate in?
  • Actuators — What actions can the agent take?
  • Sensors — What inputs can the agent perceive?

PEAS Example: Self-Driving Taxi

PEAS ComponentDescription
PerformanceSafe trip, fast, comfortable, legal, profitable
EnvironmentRoads, traffic, pedestrians, weather, passengers
ActuatorsSteering, brakes, accelerator, horn, signals
SensorsCameras, GPS, LIDAR, speedometer, microphone

Task Environment Properties

PropertyMeaningExample
Fully vs Partially ObservableCan the agent see all relevant info?Chess (full) vs Poker (partial)
Single vs Multi-agentOne or multiple agents interacting?Crossword (single) vs Chess (multi)
Deterministic vs StochasticIs the next state fully determined by current action?Chess (deterministic) vs Driving (stochastic)
Episodic vs SequentialDoes each decision depend on previous ones?Image classification (episodic) vs Chess (sequential)
Static vs DynamicDoes the environment change while agent thinks?Crossword (static) vs Driving (dynamic)
Discrete vs ContinuousFinite or infinite states/actions?Chess (discrete) vs Driving (continuous)
Known vs UnknownDoes the agent know the rules/physics?Chess (known) vs Exploration (unknown)

Exam Questions — Unit 2

Q1: What is a rational agent? How does it differ from a simple reflex agent?

Answer: A rational agent selects actions that maximize its expected performance measure. A simple reflex agent only reacts to the current percept with pre-defined rules, with no consideration of optimality or future states.

Q2: Explain the PEAS framework with an example. (5 marks)

Answer: PEAS stands for Performance, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. It is used to describe the task environment for any AI agent. Example: for a medical diagnosis system — Performance: correct diagnosis rate; Environment: patient symptoms, test results; Actuators: diagnosis output, prescription; Sensors: patient data input.

Q3: Compare all five types of AI agents. (10 marks)

Answer: See the detailed comparison above. Key progression: Simple Reflex → Model-Based → Goal-Based → Utility-Based → Learning Agent. Each adds more capability but also more complexity.

Q4: What are the properties of task environments? Explain each with an example.

Answer: Use the properties table above. Each property affects how complex the AI agent needs to be. Fully observable + deterministic environments are simplest; partially observable + stochastic + dynamic are hardest.

chapters.title: Unit 3: State Space Search
chapters.content:
Unit 3: State Space Search

12 Marks

What is State Space Search?

Many AI problems can be solved by searching through all possible states of the problem to find the solution.

State: A snapshot of the problem at a particular moment
State Space: All possible states the problem can be in
Initial State: Where we start
Goal State: Where we want to reach
Operators/Actions: What we can do to move from one state to another

Simple Example: 8-Puzzle

In the 8-puzzle (3×3 grid with 8 numbered tiles and 1 blank), the state is the current arrangement of tiles. Search means trying different moves (up/down/left/right of blank) until we reach the goal arrangement.

Properties of Search Algorithms

PropertyMeaningSimple Explanation
CompletenessWill it always find a solution if one exists?Does it guarantee to find the answer eventually?
OptimalityWill it find the best (lowest cost) solution?Does it find the shortest/cheapest path?
Time ComplexityHow much time does it take?How many nodes does it explore?
Space ComplexityHow much memory does it need?How many nodes does it store?
In complexity, b = branching factor (avg children per node), d = depth of shallowest solution, m = max depth of tree.

Uninformed Search (Blind Search)

These algorithms search without any domain-specific knowledge. They don't know how close they are to the goal.

1. Depth-First Search (DFS)

Strategy: Go as deep as possible before backtracking.

Algorithm DFS(node):
  if node is goal: return SUCCESS
  for each child of node:
    push child onto STACK
  return DFS(stack.pop())

Data Structure: Stack (LIFO)
Complete? No (can get stuck in infinite loops)
Optimal? No
Time: O(b^m)
Space: O(bm) — only stores current path, very memory efficient

When to use: When memory is limited, or you just need any solution (not necessarily optimal).

2. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Strategy: Explore all nodes at current depth before going deeper.

Algorithm BFS(root):
  queue = [root]
  while queue not empty:
    node = queue.dequeue()
    if node is goal: return SUCCESS
    for each child of node:
      queue.enqueue(child)

Data Structure: Queue (FIFO)
Complete? Yes (if branching factor is finite)
Optimal? Yes (finds shallowest goal first — optimal if all steps cost 1)
Time: O(b^d)
Space: O(b^d) — stores ALL nodes at current depth — can be huge

When to use: When you need the shortest path and memory isn't a concern.

3. Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search (IDDFS)

Strategy: Run DFS with depth limit 0, then 1, then 2... until solution found. Combines BFS's completeness with DFS's memory efficiency.

for depth = 0 to infinity:
  result = DLS(root, depth)  # Depth-Limited Search
  if result != CUTOFF: return result

Complete? Yes
Optimal? Yes (if step costs are equal)
Time: O(b^d) — nodes near root are explored multiple times but this is acceptable
Space: O(bd) — memory efficient like DFS
Best of both worlds! This is often the preferred uninformed search.

4. Uniform-Cost Search (UCS)

Strategy: Expand the node with the lowest path cost so far. Uses a priority queue.

Complete? Yes
Optimal? Yes (finds cheapest solution)
When to use: When step costs are different (e.g., roads of different lengths).

Informed Search (Heuristic Search)

These algorithms use domain knowledge — a heuristic function h(n) — to estimate how close a state is to the goal. This makes search much faster.

Heuristic h(n): An estimate of the cost from node n to the goal. It should be fast to compute and never overestimate (admissible).

Best-First Search

Strategy: Always expand the node that appears closest to the goal based on h(n).

Also called Greedy Best-First Search. It's fast but not optimal — it can get fooled by misleading heuristics.

A* Search — The Gold Standard

A* combines UCS (actual cost) and Best-First (estimated remaining cost):

f(n) = g(n) + h(n)

where:
  g(n) = actual cost from start to node n
  h(n) = estimated cost from n to goal
  f(n) = estimated total cost of solution through n

A* always expands the node with the lowest f(n) value.

Complete? Yes
Optimal? Yes (if h(n) is admissible — never overestimates)
Example heuristic for 8-puzzle: Manhattan distance (sum of horizontal + vertical distances each tile is from its goal position)

A* Example: Romania Map Problem

Finding shortest path from Arad to Bucharest:
g(Arad) = 0, h(Arad) = 366 → f = 366
Expand Arad → Zerind (g=75, h=374→f=449), Sibiu (g=140, h=253→f=393), Timisoara (g=118, h=329→f=447)
Expand Sibiu → Fagaras (g=239, h=176→f=415), Rimnicu (g=220, h=193→f=413)...
...eventually finds: Arad→Sibiu→Rimnicu→Pitesti→Bucharest (total 418)

Beam Search

Strategy: Like BFS but only keeps the best k nodes at each level (beam width k). Sacrifices completeness/optimality for memory efficiency.

Use case: Natural Language Processing, speech recognition where state space is huge.

Comparison Table — All Search Algorithms

AlgorithmCompleteOptimalTimeSpace
DFSNoNoO(b^m)O(bm)
BFSYesYes*O(b^d)O(b^d)
IDDFSYesYes*O(b^d)O(bd)
UCSYesYesO(b^(C*/ε))O(b^(C*/ε))
Greedy BFSNoNoO(b^m)O(b^m)
A*YesYesExponentialO(b^d)

Exam Questions — Unit 3

Q1: What is a state space? Define initial state, goal state, and operators with an example.

Answer: State space is the set of all states reachable from the initial state. Example: 8-Puzzle. Initial state = given arrangement; Goal state = tiles in order 1-8; Operators = move blank up/down/left/right.

Q2: Explain BFS with algorithm and properties. (6 marks)

Answer: See BFS section above. BFS uses a queue, is complete and optimal (equal step costs), but requires O(b^d) space making it impractical for large depths.

Q3: What is A* search? What makes it optimal?

Answer: A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n). It is optimal if h(n) is admissible (never overestimates the true cost). Admissibility ensures A* never "gives up" on a path that might be optimal.

Q4: Compare DFS and BFS. When would you use each?

Answer: DFS uses O(bm) space (efficient), BFS uses O(b^d) space (heavy). Use DFS when memory is limited or any solution suffices. Use BFS when shortest path is needed and tree isn't too deep.

Q5: What is IDDFS? Why is it considered best among uninformed searches?

Answer: IDDFS repeatedly runs depth-limited DFS with increasing depth limits. It has BFS's completeness and optimality, but DFS's O(bd) space efficiency. For most purposes, IDDFS is the preferred uninformed search algorithm.

chapters.title: Unit 4: Logic and Inferences
chapters.content:
Unit 4: Logic and Inferences

12 Marks

Knowledge-Based Agents

A Knowledge-Based Agent (KBA) maintains an internal knowledge base (KB) — a set of facts and rules represented in a formal language — and uses inference to derive new facts and make decisions.

KB = {known facts + rules}
Query → Inference Engine → Answer
KB + Query → TELL/ASK → Actions

Two operations on KB:

  • TELL — Add new information to the KB
  • ASK — Query the KB for information

Propositional Logic

Propositional logic deals with propositions — statements that are either TRUE or FALSE.

Symbols and Connectives

SymbolNameMeaningExample
¬NOT (Negation)Opposite¬P = "P is false"
∧AND (Conjunction)Both trueP ∧ Q
∨OR (Disjunction)At least one trueP ∨ Q
→IMPLIES (Implication)If P then QP → Q
↔BICONDITIONALP iff QP ↔ Q

Truth Table Example

P    Q    P∧Q   P∨Q   P→Q   ¬P
T    T     T     T     T     F
T    F     F     T     F     F
F    T     F     T     T     T
F    F     F     F     T     T
P→Q is FALSE only when P is TRUE and Q is FALSE. Think of it as a promise: "If it rains, I'll carry an umbrella." The promise is broken ONLY if it rained and you didn't carry one.

Limitations of Propositional Logic

Cannot represent statements about individuals in a general way. "All students are smart" cannot be easily expressed without listing every student.

First-Order Logic (FOL / Predicate Logic)

FOL extends propositional logic with:

  • Objects — things in the world (e.g., Aayan, HPU, India)
  • Predicates — properties of objects (e.g., Student(Aayan), Teacher(x))
  • Functions — mappings (e.g., FatherOf(Aayan) = Parmar)
  • Quantifiers — statements about all or some objects

Quantifiers

∀x Student(x) → HasRollNo(x)
  "For ALL x, if x is a student, then x has a roll number"

∃x Student(x) ∧ Smart(x)
  "There EXISTS at least one x who is both a student and smart"

FOL Example

Facts:
  Parent(Tom, Bob)       # Tom is parent of Bob
  Parent(Tom, Liz)       # Tom is parent of Liz
  Married(Tom, Sue)      # Tom is married to Sue

Rule:
  ∀x,y,z Parent(x,y) ∧ Parent(x,z) ∧ ¬(y=z) → Sibling(y,z)
  # If x is parent of y and z (different), then y and z are siblings

Inference:
  Sibling(Bob, Liz)      # Derived automatically

Fuzzy Logic

Classical logic: everything is TRUE (1) or FALSE (0).
Fuzzy Logic: truth values can be anywhere between 0 and 1.

Example: "It is hot today."

  • Classical: Hot OR Not Hot (binary)
  • Fuzzy: 35°C → hot(0.9), 25°C → hot(0.4), 15°C → hot(0.1)

Use cases: Air conditioning control, washing machine settings, camera auto-focus

Soundness and Completeness

  • Sound: Every statement proved by the system is actually true. (No false conclusions)
  • Complete: Every true statement can be proved by the system. (No missing conclusions)

A good inference system should be both sound AND complete.

Inference Rules

Modus Ponens (The most important!)

IF (P → Q) AND P is true, THEN Q must be true.

Example:
  Rule: IF it rains THEN ground is wet    (Rain → Wet)
  Fact: It is raining                      (Rain)
  Conclusion: Ground is wet               (Wet)  ✓

Modus Tollens

IF (P → Q) AND Q is false, THEN P must be false.

Example:
  Rule: IF it rains THEN ground is wet    (Rain → Wet)
  Fact: Ground is NOT wet                 (¬Wet)
  Conclusion: It did NOT rain             (¬Rain)  ✓

Forward Chaining (Data-Driven)

Start from known facts, apply rules, derive new facts until goal is reached.

Known: A, B
Rules: A → C,  B ∧ C → D,  D → Goal

Step 1: Apply A→C → Add C to KB
Step 2: Apply B∧C→D → Add D to KB  
Step 3: Apply D→Goal → GOAL REACHED ✓

Used in: Production systems, expert systems

Backward Chaining (Goal-Driven)

Start from the goal, work backwards to see if facts support it.

Goal: Prove D
  D requires: B ∧ C
    B: Already in KB ✓
    C: requires: A
      A: Already in KB ✓
  Therefore D is proven ✓

Used in: Prolog, diagnostic systems

Probabilistic Reasoning

Real-world reasoning involves uncertainty. Probabilistic reasoning uses probability theory to handle this.

Bayes' Theorem:

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B)

Example: Medical Diagnosis
  P(Disease|Positive Test) = P(Positive Test|Disease) × P(Disease) / P(Positive Test)
  
If test accuracy = 99%, disease prevalence = 0.1%:
  P(Disease|Positive) ≈ 9%  ← Surprising! Most positives are false positives!

Expert Systems

An Expert System is an AI program that emulates the decision-making ability of a human expert in a specific domain.

Components

  • Knowledge Base — Facts and rules from the expert
  • Inference Engine — Applies rules to facts to draw conclusions
  • User Interface — Interacts with the user
  • Explanation Facility — Explains how it reached conclusions

Famous Expert Systems

SystemDomainYear
MYCINBlood disease diagnosis + treatment1972
DENDRALChemical compound identification1965
XCONComputer system configuration1980

Exam Questions — Unit 4

Q1: Explain Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens with examples. (6 marks)

Answer: Modus Ponens: P→Q, P ∴ Q. Modus Tollens: P→Q, ¬Q ∴ ¬P. See detailed examples above.

Q2: What is Forward and Backward Chaining? When would you use each?

Answer: Forward chaining starts from facts and derives the goal (good when many possible goals). Backward chaining starts from the goal and verifies facts (good when one specific goal and few relevant rules).

Q3: What is fuzzy logic? How does it differ from classical logic?

Answer: Classical logic uses binary truth (0 or 1). Fuzzy logic allows partial truth (0 to 1). Example: "tall" is not binary — someone can be 0.7 tall. Used in control systems where gradual responses are needed.

Q4: Describe an Expert System with its components.

Answer: Expert system mimics human expert reasoning. Components: Knowledge Base (facts+rules), Inference Engine (applies rules), User Interface, Explanation Facility. Example: MYCIN diagnosed bacterial blood infections with rules like IF organism is gram-negative AND site is blood THEN organism is E.coli (confidence 0.7).

chapters.title: Unit 5: Machine Learning
chapters.content:
Unit 5: Machine Learning

12 Marks

What is Machine Learning?

Machine Learning (ML) is a subset of AI where systems learn from data to improve their performance on a task without being explicitly programmed.

"A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T and performance measure P, if its performance at task T improves with experience E." — Tom Mitchell

Classic Example: Email spam filter. You don't write rules like "if subject contains 'FREE MONEY' then spam". Instead, you feed thousands of spam and non-spam emails, and the system LEARNS the patterns.

PAC Learning Model

PAC = Probably Approximately Correct

PAC learning is a theoretical framework that defines when and how a machine learning algorithm can be said to "learn" successfully.

  • Probably: With high probability (1-δ), the learned hypothesis will be correct
  • Approximately: The hypothesis may have a small error rate (ε)
  • Correct: The learned hypothesis is close to the true target concept

Intuitively: Given enough training examples, a PAC-learnable concept can be approximated well with high confidence. Like how studying many past exam papers gives you "probably approximately correct" predictions for the next exam.

Forms of Learning

1. Supervised Learning

Learning from labeled examples — each training example has an input AND the correct output (label).

Training Data:
  Email: "Win a FREE iPhone!" → Label: SPAM
  Email: "Meeting at 3pm"    → Label: NOT SPAM
  Email: "Claim your prize"  → Label: SPAM
  
Model learns: patterns that indicate spam
Test: New email → Model predicts: SPAM or NOT SPAM

Types:

  • Classification: Output is a category (spam/not spam, cat/dog, disease/no disease)
  • Regression: Output is a number (house price, temperature, stock price)

Algorithms: Linear Regression, Decision Trees, Neural Networks, SVM

2. Unsupervised Learning

Learning from unlabeled data — no correct answers provided. The algorithm finds patterns and structure on its own.

Input: 1000 customer purchase records (no labels)
Output: Customers grouped into clusters:
  Cluster 1: Young, tech-savvy, buys electronics
  Cluster 2: Families, buys household items
  Cluster 3: Seniors, buys health products

Use cases: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, data compression
Algorithms: K-Means Clustering, PCA, Autoencoders

3. Reinforcement Learning

An agent learns by interacting with an environment, receiving rewards for good actions and penalties for bad ones.

Environment → Agent takes action → Gets reward/penalty → Learns better policy
   
Example: Training a robot to walk:
  Take step → Don't fall → +reward
  Take step → Fall → -penalty
  Over millions of attempts → learns to walk efficiently

Key concepts:

  • Agent: The learner/decision maker
  • Environment: What the agent interacts with
  • State: Current situation
  • Action: What the agent does
  • Reward: Feedback signal
  • Policy: Strategy (state → action mapping)

Famous example: AlphaGo learned to play Go better than any human through reinforcement learning.

Linear Regression

Used for predicting a continuous output from one or more inputs.

y = mx + b   (simple linear regression)
y = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + b  (multiple regression)

Example: Predict house price from size
  Training data: (1000sqft, ₹50L), (1500sqft, ₹70L), (2000sqft, ₹90L)
  Learned: price = 0.04 × size + 10  (in lakhs)
  Predict: 1200sqft → ₹58L

Cost Function: Mean Squared Error (MSE) — measures average squared difference between predicted and actual values. Training minimizes this.

Decision Trees

A tree-like model where each internal node tests an attribute, branches represent outcomes, and leaves are predictions.

Should I play tennis today?

            Outlook?
           /    |    
        Sunny  Overcast  Rain
          |       |       |
       Humidity? YES  Windy?
       /             /    
    High   Normal   True   False
     NO      YES     NO     YES

Building a tree: Use information gain or Gini impurity to select the best attribute at each split.

Neural Networks — Biological Inspiration

Biological Neuron

The brain has ~86 billion neurons. Each neuron:

  • Receives signals through dendrites
  • Processes them in the cell body (soma)
  • Sends output through the axon
  • Connects to next neuron through synapses

Artificial Neuron (Perceptron)

Inputs:  x₁, x₂, x₃
Weights: w₁, w₂, w₃  (how important each input is)
Bias:    b

Weighted Sum: z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃x₃ + b
Activation:   output = activation_function(z)

If z > threshold → fire (output 1)
If z ≤ threshold → don't fire (output 0)

Perceptron — The First Neural Network

Invented by Frank Rosenblatt in 1957. A single-layer network that can classify linearly separable data.

Example: AND gate as perceptron
  Inputs: x1, x2 (0 or 1)
  Target: x1 AND x2
  
  Weights: w1=1, w2=1, threshold=1.5
  
  x1=0, x2=0: 0+0=0 < 1.5 → output 0 ✓
  x1=1, x2=0: 1+0=1 < 1.5 → output 0 ✓  
  x1=0, x2=1: 0+1=1 < 1.5 → output 0 ✓
  x1=1, x2=1: 1+1=2 > 1.5 → output 1 ✓

Limitation: Cannot solve XOR (not linearly separable) → led to development of multi-layer networks.

Artificial Neural Network (ANN) — Feedforward Multi-Layer Perceptron

Input Layer → Hidden Layer(s) → Output Layer

[x1]  →  [h1]  →
[x2]  →  [h2]  →  [output]
[x3]  →  [h3]  →
  • Input layer: Receives raw features (e.g., pixel values)
  • Hidden layers: Learn intermediate representations (feature detection)
  • Output layer: Produces final prediction
  • Activation functions: ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh — add non-linearity

Training a Neural Network — Backpropagation

1. Forward Pass: Input → compute output
2. Calculate Loss: How wrong was the prediction?
3. Backward Pass: Compute gradient of loss w.r.t. each weight
4. Update Weights: w = w - learning_rate × gradient
5. Repeat until loss is small

This is called Gradient Descent. Think of it like walking downhill in a foggy landscape — at each step, go in the direction of steepest descent.

Exam Questions — Unit 5

Q1: What is Machine Learning? Explain its types with examples. (10 marks)

Answer: ML is learning from data without explicit programming. Three types: (1) Supervised — labeled data, e.g., spam filter. (2) Unsupervised — unlabeled data, e.g., customer clustering. (3) Reinforcement — reward-based, e.g., game playing AI.

Q2: Explain the Perceptron model. What are its limitations?

Answer: Perceptron is a single artificial neuron: computes weighted sum of inputs, applies threshold. Limitation: can only solve linearly separable problems (cannot learn XOR). Solution: multi-layer perceptrons.

Q3: What is backpropagation? Why is it important in neural network training?

Answer: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight by applying the chain rule of calculus. These gradients tell us how to adjust each weight to reduce error. It is the fundamental algorithm for training deep neural networks.

Q4: What is the PAC learning model?

Answer: PAC learning provides a formal framework for when learning is feasible. A concept is PAC learnable if for any accuracy ε and confidence δ, there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that produces a hypothesis with error ≤ ε with probability ≥ 1-δ given enough training samples.
